content_blocks.text: Before the end of the standstill period, an unsuccessful bidder puts us on notice that it has issued court proceedings. Can we award the contract anyway?
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
Before the end of the standstill period, an unsuccessful bidder puts us on notice that it has issued court proceedings. Can we award the contract anyway?

content_blocks.text: No. If a claim form has been issued in relation to legal proceedings on the decision to award a contract, this has the effect of "automatically suspending" the contract award until a court has considered the claim, and the contracting authority is not permitted to enter into the contract. If any relevant formal court proceedings have been issued, urgent legal advice should be sought.

content_blocks.text: Is it right that, once a contract has been awarded, a bidder's only remedy is damages?
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
Is it right that, once a contract has been awarded, a bidder's only remedy is damages?

content_blocks.text: No, there is a remedy of ineffectiveness, which can be awarded in certain limited circumstances (see below), even after the contract has been entered into. There are additional time limits relating to bringing an ineffectiveness claim (see above).
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015

content_blocks.text: We made a mistake in the procurement process, but the outcome was the right one. Does this matter?
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
We made a mistake in the procurement process, but the outcome was the right one. Does this matter?

content_blocks.text: Potentially, yes. Cases have suggested that in certain circumstances a bidder may have a claim even where they are unable to establish that, other than for a breach of the Regulations, they would have been likely to be successful.

content_blocks.text: What remedies are available to suppliers if we are found to have breached the Regulations?
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
What remedies are available to suppliers if we are found to have breached the Regulations?

content_blocks.text: If a court finds that the Regulations have been breached, it may declare the contract ineffective, shorten the contract, and fine the contracting authority. In addition, a bidder may claim damages for its losses resulting from the breach.

content_blocks.text: When might a contract be declared ineffective?
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
When might a contract be declared ineffective?

content_blocks.text: There are three main circumstances when this remedy may be available to suppliers.
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
When might a contract be declared ineffective?

content_blocks.text: Firstly, where the contracting authority has directly awarded a contract without placing an FTS advertisement in circumstances where an FTS advertisement is required by the legislation.
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
When might a contract be declared ineffective?

content_blocks.text: Secondly, where there has been a breach of the rules relating to the standstill period and that breach has denied the supplier an opportunity to challenge the contract award in relation to a separate, earlier breach.
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
When might a contract be declared ineffective?

content_blocks.text: Thirdly, where a call-off contract under a framework agreement for goods or services with a value over the procurement threshold has been entered into without following the relevant call-off procedures under that framework.
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
When might a contract be declared ineffective?

content_blocks.text: When could we be fined?
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
When could we be fined?

content_blocks.text: A court is required to impose a fine (described in the legislation as a "civil financial penalty") in any circumstances where the court declares a contract ineffective. A court could also impose a fine in any proceedings where the Court is satisfied that the contract has been entered into in breach of any requirement imposed by regulation 87 (i.e. the requirement to hold a standstill period), 95 or 96(1)(b) (both around the automatic suspension mechanism), without making a declaration of ineffectiveness (whether because none was sought or because the Court is not satisfied that any of the grounds for ineffectiveness applies).
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
When could we be fined?

content_blocks.text: What will the level of fine be?
heading_path: Remedies and challenges under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
FAQs
What will the level of fine be?

content_blocks.text: There is no prescribed "tariff" for fines. However, the Regulations do state that fines must be "effective, proportionate and dissuasive".
